messages.content: We lost power for almost 14 hours last night after that windstorm, whole neighborhood was dark. Kids thought it was fun for about an hour and then got bored out of their minds.

Fourteen hours is a rough stretch, especially with kids who burn through the novelty of candlelight and board games pretty fast. Did you lose everything in the fridge or did it hold on okay? That's usually the part that stings most after these longer outages, since a full freezer can generally hold safe temperatures for close to two days if you don't open it, but a fridge on its own starts becoming a gamble after about four hours.

Fridge stuff we ended up tossing just to be safe, freezer seemed fine since we barely opened it. Honestly the worst part was just not knowing when it would come back, we kept checking the utility's outage map obsessively.

That uncertainty is genuinely one of the harder parts psychologically, way more than the actual inconvenience of no lights. There's something about not having an end time that makes people restless in a way a scheduled outage wouldn't. Glad the freezer held up at least, tossing everything in the fridge is annoying but way better than the alternative of a stomach bug from spoiled food. Hopefully the windstorm damage gets cleared out around your area soon so it's less likely to happen again with the next storm that rolls through.
I'm a beginner at chess. what are the actual principles behind good opening play, not just memorizing lines?

Three big ideas cover most of it. First, control the center - pawns and pieces that influence the central squares give you more space and flexibility for your pieces to maneuver. Second, develop your minor pieces before moving the same piece twice or bringing your queen out early - wasting tempo lets your opponent develop faster and seize initiative. Third, castle reasonably early to get your king to safety and connect your rooks, unless there's a concrete tactical reason to delay it. A lot of beginner mistakes come from ignoring one of these - like pushing too many pawns without developing pieces, or chasing a pawn grab with the queen while your opponent develops three pieces and starts attacking.
is it bad to develop knights before bishops or does it not matter

There's a mild general guideline of knights before bishops, mainly because a knight's best square is often clear early, whereas a bishop's ideal diagonal can depend on how the pawn structure develops, so committing it too early can mean redeploying it later. But it's a soft guideline, not a rule - plenty of strong openings develop a bishop first when there's a clear good square, like a fianchetto setup you want to get to early.
where does the word salary actually come from? I heard something about salt

That's a popular etymology and it's mostly right, though the details get exaggerated sometimes. Salary comes from Latin salarium, which is tied to sal, meaning salt. The common story is that Roman soldiers were paid in salt because it was valuable for preserving food, but most historians now think it's more likely that salarium referred to an allowance given to soldiers specifically to buy salt, rather than salt itself being handed over as payment. Salt was indeed a valuable commodity in the ancient world - used for preservation, trade, and even religious rituals - so the connection between wages and salt makes sense even if the literal paid-in-salt version is probably folk etymology layered on top of a real linguistic root.
is salad related too then?

Yes, actually - salad traces back to the Latin herba salata, meaning salted vegetables, since Romans commonly seasoned raw greens with a brine or salt dressing. That passed through Old French salade before entering English. So salary and salad are etymological cousins, both rooted in sal, even though they ended up describing completely unrelated things in modern usage.
I noticed tiny white fuzzy spots on my pothos, kind of like little cotton balls clustered near the stem joints. Is this a disease or a bug, and how do I get rid of it?

That description, small white cottony clusters specifically near stem joints and leaf junctions, is a very classic description of mealybugs, a common houseplant pest, not a disease, and the good news is they're very treatable if caught reasonably early like it sounds like you have. Mealybugs are small soft-bodied insects that cover themselves in a white, waxy, cotton-like secretion for protection, which is exactly what you're seeing clustered in those joint areas, they specifically favor these hidden, protected nooks because it's harder for predators, and your inspection, to spot them there. First step, isolate the plant from any others nearby immediately, mealybugs spread readily to neighboring plants through contact or even just proximity, so this prevents a small problem becoming a whole-collection problem while you treat it. Treatment: dip a cotton swab in rubbing alcohol (isopropyl, 70% is fine) and directly dab each visible cluster, the alcohol dissolves their protective waxy coating and kills them on contact quite effectively, do a full pass over the entire plant, checking undersides of leaves and all stem joints carefully since they hide well. Follow this a few days later with a full plant treatment of insecticidal soap or neem oil spray, covering the whole plant thoroughly including leaf undersides, since alcohol swabbing handles what's visible but eggs or newly hatched nymphs you missed can repopulate if you don't follow up with a broader treatment.
How many rounds of treatment should I expect to need before it's actually fully gone, and how do I know when it's safe to put the plant back near my others?

Mealybugs are persistent specifically because their eggs are protected and can hatch in waves over several weeks, so a single treatment, even a thorough one, usually isn't sufficient, plan on a repeating treatment cycle rather than a one-time fix. A typical realistic timeline: do the alcohol swab plus full neem oil or insecticidal soap spray treatment as your first round, then repeat the full spray treatment every 7-10 days for at least 3-4 rounds total, even if the plant looks clean after just one or two rounds, since newly hatched nymphs from eggs that survived the first treatment often aren't visible yet but will appear within that timeframe if you stop too early. Continue this cycle until you've had at least two consecutive treatment checks, roughly 2-3 weeks, with zero new mealybugs spotted anywhere on the plant, including a close inspection of stem joints, leaf undersides, and even the soil surface where they can sometimes hide near the base. For safely reintroducing it to your other plants, I'd be conservative given how easily these spread, keep it isolated for the full duration of treatment, and only reintroduce it after that clean 2-3 week stretch with no new sightings across multiple inspections, not just after the first treatment looks successful. While it's isolated, it's also worth doing a one-time close inspection of the plants that were previously near it, just to catch any early spread you might have missed before isolating, since a few days or weeks of proximity before you noticed the infestation is enough time for mealybugs to have potentially moved to a neighboring plant already.

why do my succulents keep dying, I water them all the time to be safe

That's actually the problem, succulents store water in their leaves and are adapted to dry, infrequent watering, so "watering a lot to be safe" is the opposite of what they need. Overwatering leads to root rot, which often looks like mushy, translucent, or yellowing leaves, easy to mistake for underwatering at first glance which makes people water even more.
how often should I actually be watering them then

Depends on the species and pot/soil, but a good general approach is to let the soil dry out completely between waterings, then water thoroughly until it drains out the bottom. In most homes that ends up being every 2-3 weeks, sometimes longer in winter when they're semi-dormant. Stick a finger in the soil before watering rather than following a fixed schedule, and make sure the pot has drainage holes since standing water is what actually causes the rot.
Went to visit my cousin's farm this weekend and accidentally brushed up against the electric fence around the cattle pasture. Did not expect it to hurt that much, holy cow.

Ha, that's basically a rite of passage for anyone visiting a working farm at least once. It's a memorable jolt but usually not dangerous on its own, since those fences are designed to give a sharp, startling pulse rather than a sustained shock, which is exactly what makes it effective at training animals to avoid it after just one or two touches without actually harming them. How's your cousin's herd doing otherwise, is this their first season running cattle or have they been at it a while?

They've had cattle for about five years now, this was actually my first time visiting during calving season though, which was really cool to see. The fence thing is just going to be a funny story I tell for years I think.

Calving season is such a great time to visit, there's nothing quite like watching a calf get up on its legs for the first time within an hour or two of being born, it's one of those things that never stops being impressive no matter how many times you see it. Sounds like a genuinely good weekend overall, even with the unexpected zap.
organizing our office gift exchange this year, want to set a good price limit and rules, last year got kind of awkward

Sorry last year was rough, happy to help set this up cleaner. A common sweet spot for price limit is $20-25, enough to get something decent without anyone feeling pressured to overspend or embarrassed by a cheap-feeling gift. Clear rules that help avoid awkwardness: set a specific theme or category (funny gifts only, something under $X, a specific niche like 'office supplies but make it fun') so people aren't guessing what's appropriate. A White Elephant or Yankee Swap format (where people can steal gifts) tends to keep energy fun and light rather than a straightforward one-to-one gift exchange which can feel more personal and prone to comparison.
we tried a straight name draw last year and someone felt like their gift was way worse than others, that's what went wrong

That's exactly the failure mode a swap-style format solves, since gift quality comparison becomes part of the fun (people fighting over the good gift) rather than a sore point tied to one specific person's gift-giving. I'd switch to White Elephant this year: everyone brings one wrapped gift within your price limit, people take turns either picking a new wrapped gift or 'stealing' an already-opened one from someone else (usually capped at 2-3 steals per gift to keep it moving), and it ends naturally once everyone's had a turn. It depersonalizes the process since nobody's gift is tied to being 'from' a specific person in an awkward comparison sense, and the stealing mechanic usually gets genuine laughs rather than quiet disappointment.

I'm a college sophomore trying to decide between staying in economics or switching to computer science. I like econ fine but I'm not passionate about it, and CS interests me more but I'm worried about starting from behind. How do people usually think through a decision like this?

This is a really common crossroads and worth thinking through a few different angles rather than just gut feeling, since both the emotional pull and the practical logistics matter here. On the practical side: sophomore year is actually still a very reasonable time to switch, you're not starting from zero the way someone switching senior year would be, and most CS programs have introductory sequences designed for students without prior background, the "behind" feeling is usually more about confidence than an actual insurmountable skills gap, especially if you're generally comfortable with logical or quantitative thinking, which studying economics suggests you likely are. Concretely map out what switching actually costs: how many additional semesters, if any, would it realistically take given credits you can transfer or overlap (some econ coursework, especially statistics and calculus, often satisfies CS prerequisites too), and whether summer courses could help close any gap without extending your overall timeline. On the passion versus practicality tension itself, it's worth being honest that "not passionate but fine" in a major you'll likely work in for years, versus "genuinely more interested" in an alternative, is a meaningful difference worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as just restlessness, especially since sustained motivation through a demanding CS curriculum specifically benefits from actual interest, the classes get harder, not easier, as you progress.
That's fair. Is there a middle ground, like double majoring or minoring instead of a full switch?

Yes, and honestly this might be worth exploring seriously before committing to a full switch either direction, since it directly addresses your stated situation, liking econ fine while being more interested in CS, without forcing a binary choice you're not fully sure about yet. A CS minor alongside your econ major is a very achievable and increasingly common path, typically requiring somewhere around 5-7 courses depending on your school, which is very feasible to complete alongside a major in your remaining time as a sophomore, especially if you can start taking an intro CS course or two this coming semester to test the fit further before committing more heavily. This combination is also genuinely valuable career-wise, not just an emotional compromise, quantitative economics plus programming skills is a strong combination for fields like data analysis, quantitative finance-adjacent roles, or economics research that increasingly relies on computational tools, so it's not merely splitting the difference, it's a legitimately marketable pairing in its own right. A full double major is also possible but worth being honest about the added course load and whether it meaningfully changes your trajectory versus a minor, for many students a well chosen minor captures most of the practical benefit (real programming skills, a credential that signals capability to employers) without the substantially heavier course load a full second major requires. I'd suggest starting with one intro CS course next semester regardless of which path you lean toward, since actually experiencing a semester of real coursework, rather than reasoning about it abstractly, will probably clarify the passion question faster than more deliberation would on its own.

My sourdough starter has been really sluggish the last week, barely doubling even after 8 hours. It smells fine, kind of tangy-sweet, no funky stuff. I keep it on the counter at room temp and feed it 1:1:1 once a day. Any idea what's going on?

A few likely culprits. First, room temperature matters a lot more than people expect: below about 70F, fermentation slows dramatically, so if your kitchen has cooled down recently (which happens a lot this time of year as seasons shift), that alone could explain sluggish rises. Try moving it somewhere warmer, like inside the microwave with the light on, near the fridge motor, or in an oven with just the light on for gentle warmth. Second, once-a-day 1:1:1 feeding might not be enough if your starter is very active and using up its food quickly, causing it to peak and fall before you check on it, which reads as sluggish when it's actually just past peak. Try feeding twice a day for a few days and see if that helps. Third, check your flour: if you switched flour brands or are using a very refined all-purpose with little bran/germ, the starter may have less to feed on. Adding a spoonful of whole wheat or rye to a feeding can give it a boost since those flours have more wild yeast and enzyme activity. Lastly, hydration ratio and container matter less but a loose lid trapping too much CO2 without any gas exchange can sometimes slow visible rise. Try a few of these and watch for a livelier rise within 2-3 days.
I did just start using a cheaper flour, that's probably it. Should I switch back gradually or all at once?

You can switch back all at once, there's no real need to taper it in. Starters are pretty resilient and will adjust to a flour change within one or two feeding cycles. Just do your next scheduled feeding with the better flour at your normal ratio, discard as usual, and watch the next rise. If you want a faster fix, you could also do one "boost" feeding with a higher proportion of whole grain flour, like a 1:1:1 ratio but subbing in 20-30% whole wheat or rye instead of all-purpose, which tends to wake up a lagging starter within a single feeding because of the extra nutrients and wild yeast population already present in whole grain flour. After that you can go back to your normal all-purpose routine. Keep an eye on rise times over the next two or three days; you should see it return to doubling within 4-6 hours if your kitchen is reasonably warm. If it's still lagging after that, temperature is probably the bigger factor and worth troubleshooting next.
Went hiking this weekend and my old compass was acting weird, kept drifting instead of settling on north. Is that just a sign it's dying or something else going on?

A few things could cause that. If it's an older liquid-filled compass, sometimes the fluid develops a tiny air bubble over the years which can throw off how freely the needle settles, and that's usually pretty visible if you look closely at the capsule. It could also just be nearby metal objects on the hike itself, things like a metal watch, a knife on your belt, or even certain mineral-rich rock formations can pull the needle around locally, which is a classic hiking mistake people make without realizing it until they retrace a wrong turn. Was there anything metal you were carrying close to it when you noticed the drifting?
Oh, I did have my phone in the same pocket, that's probably it. Kind of embarrassing given how long I've been hiking honestly.

That's almost certainly it, and honestly it's one of the most common compass mistakes even among pretty experienced hikers, since phones have several small magnetic components inside them for things like the speaker and any camera stabilization, and that's more than enough to noticeably deflect a compass needle at close range. It's an easy one to overlook exactly because it seems like such a mundane object to cause interference. Good habit going forward is just keeping the compass a good distance from your phone, keys, or anything else metal whenever you're actually taking a bearing, even a foot or so of separation usually clears up the problem completely.

I've been reading about determinism and free will and it's honestly making me feel weirdly anxious, like if everything is predetermined then nothing I do matters. Can you help me actually understand the different positions here, not just the scary version I've been spiraling about?

That anxious spiral is a really common reaction to first encountering hard determinism specifically, and it's worth knowing upfront that the "nothing matters" conclusion isn't actually where most serious philosophical positions on this land, even among philosophers who accept determinism, so let's walk through the actual landscape rather than just the one alarming conclusion. Hard determinism holds that every event, including every human decision, is the necessary result of prior causes, given the state of the universe and its laws, only one outcome was ever possible, meaning free will in the sense of "could have done otherwise" is an illusion. This is the position that tends to trigger the anxiety you're describing. But there are two other major positions worth knowing. Libertarian free will (unrelated to the political term) holds that genuine free will exists and is incompatible with determinism being fully true, that at the moment of choice there's a real, undetermined branching point where you could have chosen otherwise, this is closer to the intuitive, everyday feeling of choice most people have. The position most professional philosophers actually hold, according to surveys of philosophers, is compatibilism, which argues that free will and determinism aren't actually in conflict at all, free will isn't about being uncaused, it's about acting according to your own reasons, desires, and values without external coercion, under this view, a decision being caused by your character, history, and reasoning is exactly what free will consists of, not something that undermines it, since the alternative, a decision caused by nothing at all, random rather than determined, wouldn't feel more free, it would just feel arbitrary.

The compatibilist view is interesting but I'm still not sure I get how it actually resolves the anxiety. Like even if my choices come from my own character, that character itself was determined by things I didn't choose, genes, upbringing, etc. Doesn't that just push the problem back a step?

That's a genuinely sharp objection and it's actually one of the most discussed challenges to compatibilism in the literature, sometimes called the "disappearing agent" or manipulation argument, so you're not missing something obvious, you've found a real fault line in the position rather than a naive gap. Compatibilists have a few responses worth knowing. One is that the objection assumes free will requires being the ultimate, uncaused source of your own character, but that standard is arguably incoherent even in principle, since literally nothing, free or not, could meet a standard of being self-caused from absolute scratch with zero prior influence, that's not a special problem for determinism, it's just what causation is, so holding free will to that impossible standard means nothing could ever count as free will under any metaphysics whatsoever, determined or not. A different, and honestly more practically useful, response reframes the whole question: rather than asking "could I have done otherwise given the exact same universe," which may be genuinely unanswerable and perhaps even meaningless, ask a more functional question, "am I the kind of system that responds to reasons, that changes behavior when given new information or reflection, that isn't being externally coerced," and by that standard, which is arguably what actually matters for holding people responsible, praising them, and for your own sense of agency day to day, you clearly do qualify, regardless of the deeper metaphysical question about ultimate origins. On the anxiety specifically, it might help to notice that this deeper question, however it resolves, changes literally nothing about your actual lived experience of deliberating, weighing options, and choosing, the phenomenology of choice remains identical either way, and most philosophers who've thought hardest about this, including committed hard determinists, report living completely normal lives with normal senses of purpose and responsibility, the abstract metaphysical fact, whichever it turns out to be, simply doesn't cash out into the lived meaninglessness that the initial spiral suggests it would.
quick german question - is there a real difference between "kennen" and "wissen" or are they basically the same as "to know"?

Real difference, not interchangeable. "Kennen" is for knowing/being familiar with a person, place, or thing through direct acquaintance — "Ich kenne diese Stadt" (I know/am familiar with this city), "Ich kenne ihn" (I know him). "Wissen" is for knowing facts or information — "Ich weiß, dass er kommt" (I know that he's coming), "Ich weiß die Antwort" (I know the answer). Rough rule: if you could rephrase the English sentence as 'I'm familiar with X,' use kennen; if it's 'I know that / I know a fact,' use wissen. English collapses both into 'know,' which is why it trips people up.

I've been doing Duolingo for Spanish for 6 months and I feel like I know a lot of words but can't actually hold a conversation. What am I missing?

This is an extremely common gap and it's not really about vocabulary size, it's that apps like Duolingo train recognition and translation in isolated sentences, which is a different skill from real-time production under conversational pressure, where you need to retrieve grammar and vocabulary quickly while also listening and responding, with no time to think through conjugation rules. The fix is deliberately practicing output under time pressure rather than more input accumulation. A few concrete changes: start doing italki or similar tutoring sessions, even just 30 minutes a week with a conversation-focused tutor, since nothing replicates the pressure and unpredictability of real conversation like an actual conversation, apps simply can't simulate the need to formulate a response in real time to something you didn't expect. Second, practice thinking in Spanish during small daily moments, narrating your actions internally in simple Spanish while making coffee or driving, which builds the retrieval speed that conversation requires without needing a partner every time. Third, shift some study time from vocabulary apps to listening to native content at a slightly-too-hard level, podcasts or shows with Spanish subtitles, since comprehension speed is often the bigger bottleneck than production, you can't respond to something you're still mentally translating word by word.
I'm nervous about the tutoring thing, I feel like I'll freeze up and embarrass myself. Any tips for getting over that?

That fear is nearly universal among learners at your stage and it's worth naming directly to a tutor at the start of your first session, something like "I'm nervous and I know I'll make mistakes, please be patient with me," which immediately changes the dynamic since a good tutor will slow down and reassure you rather than you silently panicking while they wonder why you've gone quiet. A few practical tricks beyond that: request a tutor who explicitly works with beginners or nervous students, most platforms let you filter or read reviews for this, and book your first session with a clear, low-stakes topic prepared in advance, like introducing yourself, your daily routine, or your hobbies, so you're not being asked fully open-ended questions with zero preparation. It also helps enormously to accept in advance that freezing up and needing a moment is completely normal and expected, not a sign you're bad at this, even fluent second-language speakers pause mid-sentence, and a decent tutor is used to sitting through silences without judgment. Consider also starting with text-based conversation practice, like a language exchange app with voice messages instead of live calls, as a stepping stone, since it removes the real-time pressure while still forcing you to produce language rather than just recognize it, then graduate to live tutoring once that feels more comfortable. The freeze-up feeling reliably fades within just a handful of sessions once your brain gets used to the format.

I keep getting confused about the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN in SQL. I understand them individually when I look them up but I can't seem to keep it straight when actually writing queries. Any way to make this click permanently?

The stickiest way to internalize this is a visual/set mental model rather than memorizing definitions, since the definitions themselves are what keeps slipping out of memory. Picture two overlapping circles, a Venn diagram, one circle for table A, one for table B, overlapping in the middle where rows match on your join condition. INNER JOIN returns only the overlapping middle section, rows that have a match in both tables, anything in either table without a match on the other side is simply dropped entirely, gone from the result. LEFT JOIN returns the entire left circle, all of table A no matter what, plus the overlapping middle where matches exist, but where table A has no match in table B, those columns from B just show up as NULL rather than the row being dropped, this is the key difference from inner join, nothing from the left table ever disappears. FULL OUTER JOIN returns the entire combined area of both circles, everything from A, everything from B, with NULLs filling in wherever a match doesn't exist on the other side, so unlike inner join, nothing from either table is ever dropped. A memory trick that helps a lot of people: with LEFT JOIN, read it as "give me everything from the left table, and whatever matches from the right, it's fine if there's nothing on the right." That plain English framing tends to stick better than the Venn diagram alone once you pair the two together.
That helps. When would I actually want a LEFT JOIN over an INNER JOIN in a real scenario, not just conceptually?

The real world signal for choosing LEFT JOIN over INNER JOIN is whenever the absence of a match is itself meaningful information you want to see in your results, rather than something you're fine silently discarding. A classic example: imagine a customers table and an orders table, and you want a report of all customers along with their most recent order. If you use INNER JOIN, any customer who has never placed an order simply vanishes from your results entirely, which is a problem if your actual goal was something like "show me all customers, including ones who haven't ordered yet, so marketing can target them with a promotion." A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders keeps every customer in the result regardless of whether they have orders, with NULL values in the order columns for customers with no orders, which you can then filter for directly, like WHERE order_id IS NULL, to specifically identify customers who've never purchased anything, a query that's structurally impossible to write correctly using INNER JOIN since those rows wouldn't exist in an inner-joined result to filter in the first place. As a general rule of thumb: use INNER JOIN when you only care about complete, matched records, like a sales report that only makes sense for actual transactions that happened, and reach for LEFT JOIN whenever one side of the relationship is your "primary" entity you want fully preserved regardless of whether a related record exists, like customers, employees, or products where the absence of related activity is meaningful business information.

need to pick a restaurant for my sister's birthday dinner, 8 people, she loves Italian food but I don't know what makes a good group-friendly Italian spot vs not

Good question to think through before booking. For a group of 8, look for places that either have a private or semi-private room, or at least large communal tables rather than a bunch of tiny 2-tops pushed together awkwardly. Family-style Italian places tend to work better for groups than plated tasting-menu spots, since sharing dishes fits the vibe and keeps the pace relaxed rather than everyone waiting on synced courses. Also worth asking when you call: whether they take reservations for that size (some places cap party reservations and want walk-ins for anything over 6), and whether they do a set menu option for large groups, which can simplify ordering and speed up service.
good point about calling ahead, what should I actually ask when I call

A short checklist: confirm they can seat 8 together (not split across tables), ask if there's a minimum spend or gratuity auto-added for large parties (common at 6+), ask about a private or semi-private area if you want one for a birthday celebration, and mention it's a birthday so they can plan a small touch like a dessert candle or card, many places are happy to do this if you tell them in advance. Also good to ask about timing — some restaurants want large parties in at a specific slot (like right at opening) rather than peak dinner rush, so you're not squeezed for time. Locking those details a day or two ahead avoids any surprises when you show up.
what's the difference between a lookahead and a lookbehind in regex, and when would I actually use one

A lookahead, written (?=...) for positive or (?!...) for negative, checks what comes after the current position without consuming those characters. A lookbehind, (?<=...) or (?<!...), checks what comes before the current position, also without consuming it. Use case: say you want to match a number only when it's immediately followed by kg but you don't want kg included in the match - you'd write something like the digits followed by a positive lookahead for kg. If instead you want to match the text right after a dollar sign without including the sign itself, you'd use a lookbehind. They're handy whenever you need to assert context around a match without that context becoming part of the captured text.
does every regex flavor support lookbehind? I remember running into issues with one language

Support is inconsistent. PCRE, Python's re module, Java, and .NET support variable-length or fixed-length lookbehind depending on version. JavaScript only added lookbehind support in ES2018, so older browsers or environments targeting older JS engines will choke on it. Some lighter regex engines, like those used in certain older grep implementations or POSIX basic regex, don't support either lookahead or lookbehind at all. If portability matters, it's often safer to capture the surrounding context in a group and just discard it in post-processing rather than relying on lookaround.
tried making bread for the first time and the dough just did not rise at all after an hour. what went wrong

Most likely culprit is the yeast, either it was dead/expired, or the water used to activate it was too hot (above roughly 120F/49C kills yeast) or too cold to activate it well. Another common issue is not enough time or too cold a room, an hour might just not be enough if your kitchen is on the cooler side, rising can take 1.5-2+ hours in a cold room.
how do I test if my yeast is actually still good before I waste another batch

Easy test: dissolve a teaspoon of sugar in about half a cup of warm water (around 105-110F, warm to the touch but not hot), sprinkle a packet or a tablespoon of yeast on top, and wait 5-10 minutes. If it gets foamy and bubbly, it's alive and good to use. If nothing happens after 10 minutes, the yeast is dead and you'll need a fresh batch before trying the bread again, no point troubleshooting anything else in the recipe until that's confirmed good.
switched my cat to a new food brand and she's basically refusing to eat it, just sniffs and walks away. is this normal

Very normal, cats are notoriously picky about food transitions, partly texture/smell sensitivity and partly just neophobia. A cold-turkey switch is the most common cause of this reaction. Try mixing a small amount of the new food in with the old, like 25% new / 75% old, and gradually shift the ratio over 7-10 days. My in-laws want to put a small electric fence around their new goat pasture to keep the goats in and coyotes out, and they've asked me to help set it up since I'm 'the tech person' in the family, which honestly just means I know how to reset a router. Before I agree to anything, what's the general idea behind how these fences actually deter animals without seriously hurting them?

The core idea is that the fence wire is connected to a device called an energizer, which periodically sends out a brief, high-voltage pulse along the wire rather than a continuous steady current. When an animal touches the wire while also in contact with the ground, its body completes a circuit back to a grounding rod, and it experiences a short, sharp, startling pulse. The pulses are deliberately brief, typically a small fraction of a second, with a relatively long gap of no current at all between pulses, which is the key design choice that makes them effective as a deterrent while avoiding the sustained, dangerous exposure you'd get from continuous household current. The unpleasant but brief zap trains animals to avoid the fence line after just a couple of encounters, which is why these fences don't need to be physically imposing barriers the way a solid wood or wire mesh fence does.

That's reassuring actually, since I was picturing something way harsher. Are there real risks I should be careful about while helping set this up, especially with grandkids who visit and might touch it out of curiosity?

It's good you're thinking that far ahead. Properly designed and installed energizers sold for home and farm use are built with safety standards specifically so a curious touch from a kid or pet produces a startling but non-dangerous experience rather than a real medical risk, but a few practical precautions still matter. Grounding needs to be installed correctly per the unit's instructions, poor grounding can make the fence less effective and occasionally behave unpredictably. It's also worth putting up simple warning signage at obvious approach points, both as a courtesy to visitors and sometimes as a legal or insurance requirement depending on the area. Finally, people with certain medical conditions like implanted pacemakers are generally advised to avoid direct contact with these fences entirely, so if that applies to anyone in the extended family, it's worth a heads-up conversation before the fence goes up rather than after.

why did linear perspective specifically emerge in renaissance italy? was nobody drawing depth before that?

Artists before the Renaissance absolutely tried to convey depth, but earlier techniques like overlapping figures, varying size somewhat intuitively, or medieval hierarchical scaling, where important figures like saints were drawn larger regardless of actual distance, weren't built on a consistent mathematical system. Linear perspective as a systematic, geometrically grounded technique is usually credited to the architect Filippo Brunelleschi in early 15th century Florence, who demonstrated that a scene's depth could be constructed by having parallel lines converge toward a single vanishing point on the horizon, mirroring how the eye actually perceives receding parallel lines like a road or a row of columns. Leon Battista Alberti then formalized this into a written treatise, giving other artists a reproducible method rather than an intuitive trick. It emerged specifically in Renaissance Florence partly because of the era's broader intellectual climate blending art with mathematics and optics, revived interest in classical Greek and Roman ideas about geometry, and patronage from wealthy families and guilds eager to fund ambitious architectural and artistic projects that rewarded this kind of technical innovation.
did that mathematical approach change how artists were trained after that, or was it more of a niche technique some used?

It became foundational fairly quickly, at least in Italy and then across Europe. Once linear perspective was formalized, it got incorporated into workshop training as a core technical skill alongside anatomy and proportion, since it gave artists a reliable method for constructing believable architectural spaces and figure placement rather than relying purely on instinct. Within a couple of generations it was assumed knowledge for any ambitious painter, and treatises on perspective, proportion, and anatomy became standard parts of an artist's theoretical education, reflecting the Renaissance ideal of the artist as someone versed in both craft and scientific principles rather than purely a manual craftsman.
what's the actual chemical difference between the fermentation that makes beer alcoholic and the one that makes yogurt sour?

They're driven by completely different organisms producing different end products from the same starting sugar. Beer fermentation is alcoholic fermentation, carried out by yeast, typically Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide through glycolysis followed by the enzyme pathway that reduces pyruvate to acetaldehyde and then to ethanol, regenerating NAD+ in the process so glycolysis can keep running without oxygen. Yogurt fermentation is lactic acid fermentation, carried out by bacteria like Lactobacillus and Streptococcus thermophilus, which convert the lactose sugar in milk into lactic acid, again regenerating NAD+ but through a different single-step reduction of pyruvate directly to lactate rather than the two-step pathway to ethanol. The lactic acid buildup is what curdles the milk proteins and gives yogurt its characteristic tang, while in beer the ethanol and CO2 are the defining products, with the CO2 also responsible for carbonation if it's trapped during fermentation.
why does muscle tissue also do lactic acid fermentation during hard exercise then, is it using bacteria?

No bacteria involved there - it's your own muscle cells running the same basic anaerobic fallback pathway, just without any microorganisms. When oxygen supply can't keep up with ATP demand during intense exercise, muscle cells can't run oxidative phosphorylation fast enough, so they shift to anaerobic glycolysis, and just like in the yogurt bacteria, they need to regenerate NAD+ to keep glycolysis running, which they do by converting pyruvate into lactate via the same type of enzyme, lactate dehydrogenase. It's essentially the same core biochemical solution to the same underlying problem, run independently by two very different kinds of cells that both need to keep glycolysis functioning without oxygen.

I'm an adult and my handwriting is honestly embarrassing, I basically write in a rushed scrawl from years of typing everything instead. Is it actually possible to meaningfully improve handwriting as an adult, or is that mostly set by childhood habits at this point?

It's genuinely very possible to meaningfully improve as an adult, handwriting is a learned motor skill, not something fixed early in life the way some people assume, and adults actually have an advantage children learning to write for the first time don't have, you already have full fine motor control and can consciously apply focused, deliberate practice rather than needing years of general motor development, which is why adults who commit to real practice often improve faster in absolute terms than the gradual multi-year process kids go through. That said, meaningful improvement does require actual deliberate practice, not just writing more in your normal daily rushed style, since practicing your existing rushed scrawl just reinforces exactly the sloppy motor patterns you're trying to change, more of the same habit doesn't retrain it. A good starting approach: get a basic handwriting workbook or drill sheet, even one aimed at kids works fine for the actual letterform practice, and spend 10-15 minutes a few times a week doing genuinely slow, deliberate letter formation practice, focusing on consistent letter size, slant, and spacing rather than speed, since speed is what caused the scrawl in the first place and needs to be temporarily removed from the equation while you rebuild cleaner underlying motor patterns. Pay particular attention to problem letters specific to you, most adults with rushed handwriting have a handful of specific letters that consistently look worst (commonly r, s, and connections between certain letter pairs), identify yours specifically and drill those individually rather than assuming uniform practice across the whole alphabet addresses your actual weak points evenly.
That's encouraging. Roughly how long would consistent practice like that take before I'd actually notice a real difference?

Most people following a consistent deliberate practice routine, something like 10-15 minutes several times a week, start noticing genuine improvement within about 3-4 weeks, and see a substantial, clearly visible difference within 2-3 months, though the exact timeline varies with how consistently you practice and how significant the starting gap was. It's worth understanding the typical progression though, since the early weeks can feel discouraging if you're expecting linear, steady improvement. The first week or two often actually feels awkward and sometimes even worse than your normal rushed writing, since you're consciously overriding an ingrained automatic motor pattern with a new, deliberate one, and anything consciously controlled initially feels clunkier than an old automatic habit, even a bad one, this is completely normal and not a sign the practice isn't working, it's actually a necessary and expected part of retraining any motor skill. By weeks three to four, the new letterforms typically start feeling more natural during slow, deliberate practice specifically, though they likely still won't transfer automatically to your fast, everyday writing yet, that transfer to natural speed is usually the last piece to click into place. Around the two month mark with consistent practice, most people find the improved forms start appearing more naturally even in normal quick note-taking, without consciously thinking about it, which is the real marker that the new pattern has actually replaced the old scrawled one at an automatic level rather than only existing as a separate "practice mode" you can access slowly but not use in daily life. Sticking with the practice even through that initial awkward-feeling stretch in the first couple weeks is honestly the part most adults give up on prematurely, right before the improvement would have started becoming genuinely visible.

What were the main structural reasons the Roman Republic collapsed, beyond just Caesar crossing the Rubicon?

The Rubicon moment was really the culmination of decades of structural strain rather than a sudden cause. A few big threads: first, the Republic's institutions were designed for a city-state, not the sprawling Mediterranean empire Rome had become by the 2nd century BCE - governors and generals far from Rome accumulated personal power and loyal armies that owed more to them than to the state. Second, the Marian reforms professionalized the army and tied soldiers' loyalty to their commanders, who promised land and pay, rather than to the Senate - this made generals like Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar into independent power brokers with private armies. Third, growing economic inequality - cheap slave labor from conquests undercut small farmers, who lost land and flooded into Rome, creating a volatile urban poor that populist politicians could mobilize. Finally, the Senate's own conservatism and unwillingness to reform (the failed attempts by the Gracchi brothers to redistribute land are a good example) meant grievances built up with no institutional outlet, so they got resolved through violence and civil war instead.
did the Gracchi reforms actually have a chance of working if the Senate hadn't blocked them?

But the deeper structural issues, like provincial governance and army loyalty, wouldn't have been touched by land reform alone, so it likely would have delayed rather than prevented the eventual crisis.

Took my nephew to the science museum this weekend and they had a huge Tesla coil demo, sparks jumping like two feet across the room, hair standing up on everyone nearby. He was obsessed and kept asking how it actually works. I gave a garbled half-answer about 'high voltage' and left it at that. Can you give me something better to tell him next time, in plain terms?

That's a great one to get a kid hooked on physics. The short version: a Tesla coil is basically two coupled coils tuned to resonate at the same frequency, so energy sloshes back and forth between them and builds up to enormous voltages, way higher than what feeds in. Once the voltage gets high enough, it overcomes the insulating resistance of the surrounding air and the whole thing dumps its stored charge in a visible arc, which is the crackling spark you saw. The reason it looks so dramatic is that the coil isn't really about current, it's about voltage and rapid oscillation, so you get spectacle without necessarily huge continuous power draw. For a kid, the coil-to-coil 'echo' idea usually lands well: imagine pushing a swing at exactly the right rhythm so each push adds to the last until it's swinging way higher than your arm ever moved.

That's a good analogy, I'll steal it. He also asked if Tesla actually wanted to send electricity through the air to power whole cities without wires. Is that a real thing he tried or is that internet mythology?

That part's real, though usually exaggerated in retellings. Tesla built the Wardenclyffe Tower on Long Island in the early 1900s specifically to test long-distance, and eventually wireless, transmission of both signals and power. His backer, J.P. Morgan, was mainly interested in the communications angle and pulled funding once it became clear Tesla's real ambition was free, ubiquitous power distribution, which had no obvious business model for a financier. The project was never finished at full scale, and most historians of science think broadcasting meaningful amounts of power that way, rather than just information, would have run into serious efficiency problems even if it had been completed. So the vision was genuine, the execution stalled for money and physics reasons both.
Do museums or performers ever do anything with that idea today, or is it strictly a history-class footnote now?

It shows up in a few fun, small-scale ways. Wireless charging pads and phone mats are a direct descendant of the coupled-coil idea, just at very short range and low power. Some science centers and hobbyists build musical Tesla coils that play recognizable tunes through the pitch of the arcs, which is a crowd favorite at demo nights. And there's a niche of stage performers, sometimes billed under names like plasma or electric music acts, who use coil arrays synced to music for a genuinely startling live show. None of it approaches Tesla's original city-scale ambition, but the coupling principle he was chasing is quietly everywhere now, just miniaturized and tamed.

I just got a pour over setup, a basic dripper and gooseneck kettle, coming from just using a regular drip machine my whole life. My first few attempts have tasted kind of sour and thin. What am I doing wrong?

Sour and thin is a very classic pour over beginner result and it points pretty specifically at under-extraction, meaning the water passed through the grounds without pulling out enough of the coffee's full flavor compounds, generally caused by one or a combination of: grind too coarse, water not hot enough, or total brew time too short. Let's go through the likely fixes in order of impact. Grind size: pour over generally wants a medium-fine grind, similar in texture to coarse sand, if you're using a grind meant for drip machines it might be too coarse for the shorter contact time of manual pour over, try grinding slightly finer and see if the sourness reduces. Water temperature: aim for 195-205F (just off a full boil, let boiled water sit about 30 seconds before pouring), water that's too cool under-extracts and tends toward sour, sharp flavors specifically. Brew time and technique: a standard pour over should take roughly 2.5-3.5 minutes total from first pour to drawdown finishing, if yours is finishing much faster than that, water is flowing through too quickly, which again under-extracts, this connects back to grind size being too coarse most commonly. Try a bloom first too: pour just enough water to saturate the grounds (roughly double the coffee's weight), wait 30-45 seconds for it to bubble and release gas, then continue your normal pour, skipping this step alone commonly causes uneven, under-extracted results.
I don't think I've been doing a bloom at all actually. Walk me through the full pour over process from start to finish with the bloom included?

Here's a full standard process for a typical single-cup pour over, adjust the coffee amount based on your dripper's size, but the ratio guidance holds generally. Start with roughly 1:16 coffee to water ratio by weight, so for a 300g final cup, use about 18-20g of coffee, medium-fine grind. Rinse your paper filter with hot water first if using one (removes papery taste and preheats the dripper), then discard that rinse water and add your grounds, giving the dripper a gentle shake to level the coffee bed. Start your timer and pour just enough hot water (195-205F) to fully saturate all the grounds, roughly 40-50g of water for that 20g of coffee, then stop and let it sit, this is the bloom, wait about 30-45 seconds while you watch it bubble and swell slightly as trapped CO2 releases. After the bloom, begin your main pour in slow, controlled circles, starting from the center and spiraling outward toward the edges then back in, avoiding pouring directly onto the filter's edge, adding water in stages, say pouring up to about half your total water, pausing briefly, then continuing to the full amount, rather than one continuous pour, though a slow continuous spiral works fine too once you're comfortable. Aim for total drawdown time, from first pour to the last water draining through, of about 2.5 to 3.5 minutes. If it finishes faster than that consistently, grind finer next time, if slower, grind slightly coarser, this dial-in process typically takes 3-5 cups of practice before it clicks.

I started keto about 2 weeks ago and I have zero energy, headaches, kind of foggy. Is this normal or did I mess something up?

What you're describing sounds very consistent with what's commonly called "keto flu," a cluster of symptoms, fatigue, headache, brain fog, sometimes irritability or nausea, that a lot of people experience in the first one to two weeks of a ketogenic diet, so this is a known and common experience, not necessarily a sign you've done something wrong, though there are a couple of likely specific causes worth addressing directly rather than just waiting it out passively. The primary driver is usually electrolyte imbalance, specifically sodium, potassium, and magnesium, when you drastically cut carbs, your body's insulin levels drop significantly, and lower insulin causes your kidneys to excrete more sodium (and water) than usual, which then also pulls potassium and magnesium out along with it, this electrolyte depletion is what's actually behind most of the fatigue, headache, and fogginess, much more than "your body adjusting to fat burning" as it's sometimes casually described. The direct fix: significantly increase your sodium intake, more than feels intuitive, many keto guides recommend somewhere around 3000-5000mg of sodium daily during this adjustment period, which is well above typical dietary guidelines but appropriate given how much you're now excreting, adding broth, salting food more liberally than usual, or even a plain glass of water with a measured amount of salt dissolved in it can meaningfully help within hours, not days. Also actively supplement potassium-rich foods like avocado and leafy greens, and consider a magnesium supplement, since these three electrolytes together typically resolve the bulk of keto flu symptoms within a day or two of correcting for them properly.
How do I know if it's actually electrolytes versus just not eating enough calories overall? I've also cut portions a bit without really meaning to.

That's a smart distinction to draw, since the two causes have overlapping symptoms but somewhat different fixes, and it's genuinely common for both to be happening simultaneously when someone starts keto, since cutting out an entire food category often unintentionally reduces overall intake too, especially if you haven't consciously replaced those calories with adequate fat and protein. A few ways to tell them apart. Timing and pattern: electrolyte-related fatigue tends to feel more acute and symptom-specific, headaches, muscle cramps or twitches, dizziness on standing up quickly (a classic sign of low sodium specifically), while general caloric insufficiency tends to feel more like persistent, flat low energy and increased hunger or preoccupation with food throughout the day, without necessarily the more acute headache or dizziness component. The most reliable way to actually distinguish them rather than guessing is simply to track for a few days, honestly log what you're eating including approximate calories, and separately track your sodium intake specifically, most people significantly underestimate both how few calories they're eating and how little sodium they're getting once they cut processed foods, which often contain a lot of hidden sodium, without deliberately compensating. Given that you mentioned unintentionally cutting portions, I'd address both simultaneously rather than trying to isolate one cause first: increase sodium as described, and separately make sure you're eating enough total food, keto specifically requires eating adequately from fat and protein sources to replace the calories that carbs used to provide, if you've simply removed carbs without adding more fat and protein to compensate, you've accidentally created a low-calorie diet on top of a ketogenic one, which compounds fatigue considerably. Aim to eat until genuinely satisfied at meals rather than restricting further, fattier cuts of meat, added oils, nuts, and full-fat dairy are all appropriate and expected to be eaten more liberally on keto specifically to prevent this exact accidental under-eating problem.

why is binary search O(log n) instead of O(n)? I get that it halves the array but I want the intuition for why that gives log n

The key intuition is thinking about how many times you can cut something in half before it's down to one element. If you start with n elements and halve the search space each step, after k steps you have roughly n divided by 2 to the k elements left. The search ends when that quantity reaches 1, which happens when 2 to the k equals n, meaning k equals log base 2 of n. So the number of halving steps grows proportionally to the logarithm of n rather than n itself. A concrete way to feel it: for a list of a million elements, log2(1,000,000) is only about 20, so binary search finds anything in about 20 comparisons max, compared to potentially a million comparisons for a linear scan.
does that mean doubling the input size only adds one more comparison on average?

Pretty much, yes, for the worst case at least. If you double n, log2(2n) equals log2(n) plus log2(2), which is just log2(n) plus 1. So doubling the array size only ever adds one additional halving step in the worst case, which is exactly why binary search scales so gracefully compared to linear-time algorithms as datasets grow large.

what's the difference between a transform boundary and the other two plate boundary types?

There are three main types based on how plates move relative to each other. Divergent boundaries are where plates move apart, allowing magma to rise and create new crust, like at mid-ocean ridges. Convergent boundaries are where plates move toward each other, which can result in one plate subducting beneath another, forming deep trenches and volcanic arcs, or in two continental plates colliding to push up mountain ranges like the Himalayas. Transform boundaries are different from both because the plates aren't moving apart or together at all, they're sliding horizontally past each other, and crust is neither created nor destroyed at this type of boundary. The San Andreas Fault in California is the classic transform boundary example, where the Pacific and North American plates grind past each other laterally, producing frequent earthquakes from the friction and stress buildup rather than volcanic activity.
why don't transform boundaries produce volcanoes the way convergent ones do?

Volcanism at convergent boundaries is driven by subduction - one plate gets forced down into the mantle, and the intense heat and pressure cause water and other volatiles carried down with the subducting plate to lower the melting point of the overlying mantle rock, generating magma that rises to the surface. Transform boundaries don't involve any plate being pushed down into the mantle or any new material rising up to fill a gap, since the plates are just sliding past each other laterally with no vertical component of motion. Without that subduction process or the upwelling that happens at divergent boundaries, there's no mechanism generating fresh magma, so transform boundaries produce lots of seismic stress and earthquakes but essentially no volcanic activity.

what's the actual difference between a 9th chord and an add9 chord?

A 9th chord implies the full stack built from the root: root, third, fifth, flat or natural seventh, and the ninth on top - so it's essentially a seventh chord with the ninth added. An add9 chord skips the seventh entirely - it's just a triad (root, third, fifth) with the ninth added directly on top, no seventh involved. So a C9 chord would be C-E-G-Bb-D, while a Cadd9 would be C-E-G-D, with no Bb at all. The sonic difference is notable - the add9 has a cleaner, more open sound since it avoids the tension of the seventh, and it's common in pop and folk voicings, while proper 9th chords show up a lot more in jazz where that seventh's tension is part of the desired color.

It's a favorite closing or coloring chord in jazz and lounge styles because it has a warm, resolved quality without the harmonic pull that a seventh would create, since there's no leading-tone tension pushing it toward another chord.

starting to run for the first time, do I actually need special running shoes or can I use whatever sneakers I have

You can technically run in any sneaker for a short time, but proper running shoes make a real difference once you're logging more than a mile or two regularly, mainly around cushioning and support tailored to the repetitive impact of running versus casual walking. Regular fashion sneakers or old worn-out shoes especially can increase risk of shin splints or knee discomfort since they weren't designed for that kind of repeated impact. what does gait fitting actually involve, is it worth the extra step

That determines whether you'd benefit from a neutral shoe, a stability shoe, or a motion-control shoe. It matters because the wrong shoe type for your gait can contribute to overuse injuries down the line as your mileage increases. Most specialty running stores do this fitting for free if you're buying shoes there, so it's low-cost enough that it's worth doing before your first real pair, even if you end up just confirming a neutral shoe is fine.

I've gotten really into a niche hobby lately, electroplating cheap costume jewelry with a thin layer of copper for an antique look, using a little kit I found online. Can you explain what's physically happening in that tank?

That's a genuinely satisfying hobby to fall into, there's something almost meditative about watching a color change happen gradually like that. The core idea is that your tank contains a solution with dissolved metal ions floating freely in it, along with two electrodes submerged in the liquid, one being the object you want plated and the other typically a piece of the actual metal you're depositing. When current runs through the setup, it drives a reaction at each electrode, at one, metal atoms from the solid electrode dissolve into the solution as ions, replenishing what's being used up, and at the other, that's your jewelry piece, dissolved metal ions in the solution gain electrons and settle back out as solid metal, building up gradually as an even coating across the surface. The whole system essentially becomes a slow, controlled transfer of metal atoms from a stock electrode onto your piece, ion by ion, which is why patience and steady conditions matter so much for getting a smooth, even result rather than one that looks blotchy.

That explains why the kit warned me not to move the jar around while it's running. Does the type of metal I'm plating with actually matter for how well it sticks, or is copper just generally an easy one to work with as a beginner?

Both things are true at once. Copper genuinely is one of the friendlier metals for hobbyists to start with, its plating chemistry is comparatively forgiving and doesn't demand extremely precise conditions to get a decent-looking result, which is exactly why beginner kits usually lead with it. But the underlying base material you're plating onto does matter a lot for how well anything sticks long-term, some materials accept a coating cleanly and hold onto it durably, while others need extra preparatory steps, like a preliminary cleaning or an intermediate coating layer, to get a metal to adhere well rather than flaking off after a few days of wear. If your costume jewelry pieces are a mixed bag of base metals, you may notice some hold the copper finish beautifully while others need a bit more surface prep before they take a coating as reliably, which is a pretty normal thing for hobbyists at your stage to run into and troubleshoot piece by piece.
That actually matches what's been happening, a couple pieces looked amazing right away and one flaked weirdly within a day. Good to know it's a prep issue and not me doing the core process wrong.

Some people also swear by a metal safety pin clipped inside a pocket, the idea being it gives accumulated charge somewhere harmless to discharge to rather than building up across the fabric. None of these are magic bullets on their own, but combining a couple, like a humidifier plus dryer balls, usually knocks it down to a much more tolerable level for most people through the dry months.

My sister needs some kind of internal imaging done for a suspected issue with her kidney and her doctor mentioned both CT and MRI as options before deciding which to schedule. MRI works through an entirely different physical principle, it doesn't use ionizing radiation at all, instead relying on a strong magnetic field to align the naturally occurring magnetic behavior of hydrogen atoms throughout soft tissue, then reading out how they respond to radio pulses to build up an image, which tends to make it particularly strong for distinguishing between different types of soft tissue with subtle differences, things a CT scan might render as a similar shade of gray.
So for a kidney issue specifically, does that mean MRI is just generally the better pick since kidneys are soft tissue, or is it more complicated than that?

It's genuinely more complicated than a blanket rule, and this is really where it becomes a judgment call for her specific doctor rather than something you or I should try to settle. MRI might get chosen instead if there's a need to characterize soft tissue detail more precisely, if she has an allergy history that makes a CT contrast dye risky, or if there's a specific reason to avoid the ionizing radiation CT involves, like if she were pregnant or scans need to be repeated frequently over time. I've been playing guitar for about 8 months, mostly self taught. I can do basic chords and simple strumming but I feel stuck. What should a practice routine actually look like to break through a plateau like this?

Plateaus at the 6-12 month mark are extremely common and usually come from practicing broadly (playing songs you already sort of know) rather than deliberately (targeting specific weak points), so the fix is restructuring practice time into distinct blocks rather than just "playing guitar" for however long. A solid 30-45 minute daily routine at your stage: 5-10 minutes of warmup, chromatic exercises or simple scale runs to build finger independence and speed without thinking about a song. 10 minutes of chord transition drills, picking your two or three worst chord changes (commonly F, B minor, or barre chords generally) and looping just that transition slowly with a metronome, gradually increasing speed only once it's clean. 10-15 minutes of strumming pattern work, deliberately practicing patterns slightly harder than what you use in songs, including syncopation and muting, since strumming feels stuck when it isn't pushed past comfort level. The remaining time on actual songs, but pick one slightly above your comfort level rather than only songs you can already play, since that's where real progress happens. Also record yourself weekly, it's uncomfortable but genuinely the fastest way to notice timing and buzzing issues you can't hear while playing.
Barre chords are definitely my weak point, I basically avoid them. Any specific tips there?

Barre chords are the single most common wall at this stage, and it's almost always a technique issue rather than a strength issue, even though it feels like you just need stronger hands. The biggest fix is thumb position: your thumb should be roughly behind your index finger on the back of the neck, not wrapped over the top, and pushing more with thumb-to-finger squeeze rather than raw finger pressure into the fretboard reduces the effort dramatically. Second, angle the barre finger slightly, using the side of the finger rather than the flat pad, since the side has a harder bone edge that presses strings down more efficiently with less muscle effort. Third, isolate practice: don't practice barre chords inside full songs yet, instead just fret an E-shape barre chord anywhere on the neck, strum once, release completely, rest, and repeat, focusing purely on getting a clean sound with minimal buzzing, maybe 5 minutes a day of just this. Your hand also needs actual physical adaptation time, calluses and small hand muscles genuinely get stronger over 2-4 weeks of consistent short practice, so don't judge progress day to day, judge it week to week. Once a single barre chord rings clean consistently, add slow chord changes into and out of it before ever trying it inside a real song at tempo.

why would anyone use quicksort over mergesort if quicksort's worst case is O(n^2)?

In practice quicksort tends to be faster on average despite that worst-case risk, mainly because of constant factors and memory behavior. Quicksort sorts in place, needing only O(log n) additional space for the recursion stack, while mergesort needs O(n) additional space for the merge step, which matters a lot for large datasets or memory-constrained environments. Quicksort also tends to have better cache locality since it works on contiguous subarrays in place, while mergesort's merge step involves more scattered memory access patterns in some implementations. The O(n^2) worst case for quicksort happens specifically with poor pivot choices, like always picking the first or last element on already-sorted or adversarially constructed input, but with randomized pivot selection or median-of-three pivoting, that worst case becomes extremely unlikely in practice, so most real-world implementations, including many standard library sort functions, use quicksort or a hybrid approach as the default.
so what do actual standard library implementations use these days?

Most modern standard libraries use hybrid approaches rather than a pure textbook algorithm. Many use introsort, which starts with quicksort but switches to heapsort if the recursion depth exceeds a threshold, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case while keeping quicksort's typical average-case speed. For small subarrays, many implementations switch to insertion sort since it has lower constant overhead for small n. Python's built-in sort, Timsort, is a different hybrid entirely, designed around merge sort and insertion sort specifically to exploit existing runs of ordered data common in real-world data, which mergesort and quicksort don't inherently take advantage of.

Each player is randomly assigned one of several distinct roles (Medic, Scientist, Researcher, and others) with a unique special ability, and since your team only has 4 of these roles active in the game at a time out of a larger pool, the specific role combination changes meaningfully game to game, which changes your team's strategy each time even though the board and win condition stay the same. The game also has adjustable difficulty via how many "epidemic" cards you include in the deck, so once your group is reliably winning on the base difficulty, you can ramp up to make it a real challenge again rather than the game simply becoming a solved, easy win every time. Most groups get a solid 15-25 plays of real enjoyment out of base Pandemic before it starts to feel like you've seen most of what it offers, and by that point there are also several standalone sequel versions (Pandemic Legacy being the most acclaimed, a version with a long-term evolving campaign) that give you a natural next step rather than the hobby dead-ending once base Pandemic runs its course.

We had a pretty wild multi-hour blackout last week after a storm knocked something out nearby, and it made me realize I have basically no idea how power actually gets to my house or what typically fails during storms like that. Can you give me the broad picture, from a power plant somewhere to the outlet in my kitchen?

Glad the blackout at least sparked some curiosity rather than just frustration, it's a genuinely interesting system once you see the full chain. Power generally starts at a plant of some kind, and immediately after generation it gets stepped way up to a very high voltage for the long haul across transmission lines, since sending electricity at higher voltage over long distances loses considerably less energy along the way compared to sending it at the lower voltage your appliances actually use. That high-voltage electricity travels across the big lattice towers you see crossing rural land and highways, and as it approaches your area, a series of substations progressively steps that voltage back down in stages, from transmission level down to a more moderate distribution level. Finally, the small pole-mounted or ground-level box near your specific street does the last step-down, bringing it to the safe, low household level that actually reaches your outlets.
So during a storm like the one we had, where in that whole chain does stuff usually actually fail? Is it more often way out at the big towers or something closer to my actual house?

For a typical residential storm-related outage, the failure is overwhelmingly more likely to be somewhere in the local distribution portion of that chain rather than out at the major long-distance transmission towers, which tend to be more robustly engineered and are a less frequent point of failure for routine severe weather. The classic culprits are things like a tree branch or falling limb taking down a local line, wind physically damaging equipment on a nearby pole, or a lightning strike causing a protective device to trip and deliberately cut power to a section of the grid as a safety measure, rather than letting a fault propagate further and cause worse damage. That's also part of why outages during storms are often patchy rather than uniform, one street loses power for hours while a neighboring one a few blocks over stays lit the whole time, because the failure point tends to be a fairly localized piece of equipment or line serving that specific area rather than something upstream shared broadly across the whole city.

I want to start making cocktails at home beyond just vodka sodas but I don't want to buy a ton of random bottles right away. What's a small, versatile bar setup that lets me make a decent range of drinks?

This is a smart way to approach it, a lot of people either buy way too much specialty stuff upfront or stick to one spirit forever, and there's a well-established minimal setup that unlocks a genuinely wide range of classic cocktails without excessive investment. For spirits, a solid starting five: a good gin (versatile, works in a huge number of classics), a bourbon or rye whiskey, a blanco or reposado tequila, a white rum, and a good vodka if you still want that option, though vodka is honestly the least versatile of the group for classic cocktail-making specifically since it's designed to be relatively flavorless. Beyond base spirits, a few modifiers do a huge amount of heavy lifting: dry vermouth and sweet vermouth (both keep in the fridge once opened, don't skip this storage step, they oxidize like wine), a orange liqueur like Cointreau or triple sec, and Angostura bitters, which despite being used in tiny amounts appear in an enormous number of classic recipes. With just this list, you can make: a Negroni (gin, sweet vermouth, Campari, a worthwhile sixth bottle to add early since it's essential to several classics), a Manhattan (rye, sweet vermouth, bitters), a Martini (gin or vodka, dry vermouth), a Margarita (tequila, orange liqueur, lime), a Daiquiri (rum, lime, simple syrup), an Old Fashioned (bourbon, sugar, bitters), and a Whiskey Sour, among many others, covering most of the foundational classic cocktail families from a genuinely compact shopping list.
Good list. Of those, which one is the most forgiving to actually make well as a total beginner, like least likely for me to mess up the ratios?

The Daiquiri is genuinely the best beginner starting point, and it's not a coincidence that it's also one of professional bartenders' favorite "test" drinks for judging a new hire's skill, precisely because its simplicity means there's nowhere to hide, but that same simplicity also makes it very forgiving and quick to dial in correctly once you know the basic ratio. The classic ratio is 2 parts rum, 1 part fresh lime juice, 3/4 part simple syrup (equal parts sugar and water, heated briefly to dissolve then cooled, keeps in the fridge for weeks), shaken hard with ice and strained into a chilled glass. The reason it's forgiving for a beginner despite only three ingredients is that the balance of sour, sweet, and strong is very intuitive to taste-test and adjust in real time, if it's too tart, add a touch more simple syrup, if it's too sweet, a touch more lime, there's no complex layering of multiple modifiers interacting in less obvious ways like a Manhattan or Negroni has, where vermouth, bitters, and spirit all shift the balance in less immediately obvious directions. One genuinely important tip regardless of which drink you start with: always use fresh-squeezed lime juice, never bottled lime juice concentrate, the difference in a Daiquiri specifically is enormous since fresh citrus has a brightness and complexity that bottled juice, which oxidizes and loses aromatic oils quickly after processing, simply can't replicate, this one substitution matters more than almost any other variable in determining whether your first attempts taste like a real cocktail or a flat, vaguely-limey sweet rum drink. Once the Daiquiri feels easy and well balanced, the Whiskey Sour uses a nearly identical ratio logic (spirit, citrus, sweetener) and is a natural next step before moving to drinks with vermouth or bitters layered in.
