I want to start meal prepping vegetarian lunches for the work week but every time I try, by Thursday everything tastes the same and I'm sick of it. How do people actually make prepped food not boring?

The Thursday fatigue almost always comes from prepping one complete dish five times rather than prepping modular components you recombine differently each day, which is the actual trick professional meal preppers use. Instead of making, say, five containers of the same vegetable stir fry, prep separate components in bulk: one grain (rice, farro, or quinoa), one or two protein sources (roasted chickpeas, baked tofu, black beans), three or four vegetables roasted or sauteed separately so their flavors stay distinct, and two or three different sauces or dressings in small jars, like a tahini lemon sauce, a spicy peanut sauce, and a basic vinaigrette. Then each day you assemble a different combination, grain plus chickpeas plus roasted broccoli plus tahini sauce on Monday, same grain plus black beans plus roasted peppers plus peanut sauce on Tuesday, and suddenly it feels like different meals even though the shopping and cooking effort was the same as making one dish five times. Varying the sauce alone does most of the heavy lifting here since sauce is what your palate registers most strongly. Also prep in appropriately different textures, something crunchy like toasted nuts or seeds sprinkled on top at the end of each meal (not prepped soggy in advance) keeps things interesting texturally even when the base ingredients repeat.
That's a good system. Do you have go-to sauce recipes that keep well in the fridge for the week?

Yes, a few reliable ones that hold up for 5-7 days refrigerated without separating badly or losing flavor. Tahini lemon sauce: whisk together a quarter cup tahini, juice of one lemon, one minced garlic clove, a splash of water to thin, and salt to taste, it'll thicken in the fridge so just add a little water to loosen before using. Spicy peanut sauce: combine a quarter cup peanut butter, two tablespoons soy sauce, one tablespoon rice vinegar, one teaspoon sriracha or chili garlic sauce, one teaspoon honey or maple syrup, and enough warm water to thin to a pourable consistency, this one is very forgiving and keeps well over a week. A basic miso vinaigrette: whisk one tablespoon white miso paste with two tablespoons rice vinegar, one tablespoon neutral oil, and a teaspoon of sesame oil, great over roasted vegetables and grains for a different flavor profile than the other two. A simple green herb sauce, blending cilantro or parsley with lime juice, olive oil, garlic, and a pinch of salt, adds brightness that cuts through heavier grain bowls and also keeps roughly a week if you add a thin layer of oil on top to limit oxidation. Rotating between these four alone, on the same base ingredients, gives you enough variety that a five day prep genuinely doesn't feel repetitive by Thursday.
I've gotten really into building my own guitars as a hobby and I'm about to hand-wind my first set of pickups. Any general tips before I start, or things people commonly mess up?

That's a great next step if you're already comfortable with the woodworking side. The biggest thing people underestimate is just how tedious and meditative the winding process is — you're talking thousands of turns of extremely thin wire around the bobbin, and doing it by hand without a winder jig can take a surprisingly long time and test your patience. Consistency in tension matters a lot too, because uneven winding tension can lead to a pickup that sounds noticeably different from one you intended to match, even if the turn count is close. A lot of first-timers also don't scatter-wind at all and end up with very uniform, machine-like winding, which actually produces a different tonal character than the somewhat irregular scatter-wound pickups vintage instruments are famous for. If you want that warmer, less bright vintage tone, deliberately letting the wire fall a little unevenly as you go is actually part of the traditional technique, not a mistake to avoid.
Interesting, I didn't realize scatter winding was intentional. What about the magnets themselves, does it matter a ton which type I use?

It does make a real audible difference, and it's one of those areas where guitar builders have strong opinions. Alnico magnets in their various grades are the classic choice and tend to give a warmer, more rounded tone with a softer high end, which is why so many vintage-style pickups use them. Ceramic magnets are stronger and cheaper, and they tend to push out a louder output with a sharper, more aggressive top end, which is popular in a lot of heavier styles of music. Beyond the material, the strength and orientation of the magnets relative to the coil also shapes the output and the way the pickup responds to how hard you pick the strings. A lot of builders end up experimenting with a couple of different combinations across their first few builds before they settle on what actually matches the sound they're chasing, so don't be discouraged if your first set doesn't sound exactly how you pictured it.
My echeveria has been getting really stretched out and leggy, leaves spaced far apart on a long stem. What's causing that and can I fix it?

That stretching, called etiolation, is almost always caused by insufficient light, the plant is literally growing toward whatever light source it can find, elongating the stem between leaves in the process, and unfortunately this growth pattern can't be reversed on the existing stem, the plant won't compact back down once it's stretched. What you can do is fix it going forward and propagate a fresh, compact rosette from the current plant. First, move it to a much brighter spot, ideally a south or west facing window with several hours of direct sun, or under a grow light if your space doesn't get much natural light, since most echeverias want quite intense light, more than people expect for a houseplant. For the existing leggy plant, you can behead it: cut the rosette off the top of the stem, leaving an inch or two of stem attached, let the cut end callus over for a few days in a dry spot out of direct sun, then place it on top of dry succulent soil (not buried) until it roots, which typically takes 2-4 weeks. The original stem left in the pot will often sprout new baby rosettes from the sides too, so you end up with more plants, not fewer, just give both pieces bright light this time around.
How do I know if the new spot is actually bright enough, or if I'm just guessing?

A decent low-tech gut check is the shadow test: hold your hand about a foot above where the plant will sit, at the time of day it'll get the most light, and look at the shadow it casts. A sharp, well-defined shadow with crisp edges generally indicates bright light suitable for sun-loving succulents, a fuzzy, soft-edged shadow indicates medium light, which is fine for many houseplants but usually still not quite enough for echeverias to stay compact, and no visible shadow at all means the spot is too dim and will cause continued stretching no matter what else you do. Beyond that, watch the plant's behavior over the following month as your real feedback signal: new leaves growing tightly against the rosette with normal spacing means the light is sufficient, while any continued stretching on new growth means you need to either move it closer to the window, remove any sheer curtains blocking light, or supplement with a grow light. If natural light is genuinely limited in your space, a inexpensive full-spectrum grow light placed 6-12 inches above the plant for 10-14 hours a day is a very reliable fix and takes the guesswork out entirely, since you can be certain of the intensity rather than estimating from a window's orientation and the season's changing sun angle.

My coworker and I got into it at lunch about whether Edison was actually a villain in the whole AC/DC war of the currents thing or if that's just internet revisionism gone too far the other way. What's your take?

I think the truth sits somewhere in the messy middle, honestly, and the internet does tend to swing hard toward one caricature or the other. Edison genuinely did some ethically dubious things during that period, like publicly funding and staging animal electrocutions using alternating current specifically to scare the public into associating AC with danger, which was a pretty transparent smear campaign against Westinghouse and Tesla's approach. That part isn't revisionist exaggeration, it's well documented. On the other hand, the modern narrative that paints Tesla purely as a saintly misunderstood genius and Edison as nothing but a thieving corporate villain flattens out a lot of real nuance too, since Edison's direct current systems weren't simply inferior in every way, they had real safety advantages at the time for local, low-voltage distribution, and his broader body of work in areas outside the current war, like recorded sound and motion pictures, is genuinely groundbreaking regardless of how messy his business tactics were.
Fair enough. Do you think Tesla gets overhyped these days as this misunderstood genius myth, kind of divorced from what he actually accomplished?

There's definitely some of that going on. His real, verifiable contributions are already remarkable enough on their own, the induction motor and his work on the polyphase AC system were genuinely transformative and arguably did more to shape the modern electrical grid than anything Edison built. But somewhere along the way, especially in certain corners of the internet, that legitimate legacy got fused with a lot of speculative and frankly pretty unfounded claims about wireless power transmission to the whole planet, death rays, and various conspiracy theories about suppressed inventions, which tend to crowd out appreciation for the concrete engineering he actually delivered. It's a bit of a shame because the real story doesn't need the embellishment, a brilliant but difficult, financially unlucky immigrant engineer who reshaped how electricity gets distributed is already a compelling enough narrative without needing him to be a misunderstood wizard on top of it.

I got a job offer that's decent but slightly below what I was hoping for. I've never actually negotiated a salary before, it feels really awkward. How do I even bring it up without seeming greedy or risking the offer?

The awkwardness is almost entirely a perception issue, not a reality one, employers generally expect negotiation at the offer stage, it's a normal, routine part of hiring, not an adversarial or unusual request, and a reasonable counter essentially never rescinds an offer, companies that would do that over a polite negotiation are rare and honestly a red flag about their culture anyway. The key to not sounding greedy is framing it around market value and enthusiasm rather than personal need or entitlement. A workable script: express genuine enthusiasm for the role first, explicitly, then note that based on your research into market rates for this role and your specific experience, you were hoping for a number somewhere in a specific range, and ask if there's flexibility. Something like: "I'm really excited about this offer and would love to move forward. Based on my research and experience level, I was hoping we could get closer to [number]. Is there room to discuss that?" This is polite, specific, and gives them an easy path to say yes or make a counter of their own. Do this over a call or in person if possible rather than email, tone carries better and reduces the chance of the ask reading as terse or demanding in writing.
What if they say the number is firm and there's no room to negotiate? Is there anything else worth asking for at that point?

If base salary is genuinely firm, that's actually a very common outcome and not the end of the conversation, there's usually room elsewhere even when the base number itself can't move, especially at companies with strict banding or budget constraints tied to the base figure specifically. Worth asking about, roughly in order of how often companies have flexibility: a signing bonus, which often comes from a completely different budget line than base salary and companies can be surprisingly flexible on this even when the base is locked. Additional PTO days, since this typically costs the company very little relative to cash compensation but is genuinely valuable to you. An earlier compensation review date, asking for a formal 6-month review instead of the standard annual one, which sets up a near-term second chance to negotiate once you've proven yourself, rather than waiting a full year. Remote or flexible work arrangements, if relevant to the role, sometimes traded for lower cash comp. Professional development budget or conference/training allowances, particularly for roles where continued learning is clearly valuable to the company too. When you ask, do it as a simple follow up: "I understand if the base number is firm, would there be any flexibility around a signing bonus or additional PTO instead?" This keeps the conversation collaborative rather than making it seem like you're just trying to extract concessions after already being told no once.

how did scholars actually manage to translate hieroglyphics if nobody had spoken the language in centuries?

The breakthrough came from the Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, which had the same decree inscribed in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic, an everyday Egyptian script, and ancient Greek, which scholars could already read fluently. Because the Greek text gave a known reference translation, scholars could work out that the hieroglyphic and Demotic versions said the same thing, and use the Greek as a key to start matching specific hieroglyphic symbols to known words and names. Jean-Francois Champollion made the decisive breakthrough in the 1820s by focusing on cartouches, the oval rings enclosing royal names, correctly guessing that the hieroglyphs inside spelled out the name Ptolemy phonetically, and cross-referencing that with a similarly enclosed name he identified as Cleopatra on a different inscription, which let him confirm that certain hieroglyphic signs functioned phonetically, representing sounds, rather than purely as ideograms representing whole concepts or objects, which had been the dominant assumption before that.
so hieroglyphics are a mix of phonetic symbols and picture-symbols then, not purely one or the other?

Exactly, and that mixed nature is part of why earlier attempts to decode it purely as a symbolic picture-language kept failing. Egyptian hieroglyphic writing combines phonograms, symbols representing individual sounds or sound combinations, with logograms representing whole words or concepts directly, and determinatives, additional symbols placed at the end of a word with no phonetic value themselves but clarifying which category of meaning the word belongs to, helping distinguish between homophones. Champollion's insight was recognizing that the system used phonetic elements extensively, especially for foreign names like Ptolemy and Cleopatra that had no pre-existing traditional logogram, which forced the scribes to spell them out sound by sound using phonetic hieroglyphs, giving him the crack he needed into the system as a whole.
someone asked me the difference between LEFT JOIN and INNER JOIN in an interview and I blanked. can you give me a clean explanation I can remember?

Sure. INNER JOIN only returns rows where there's a match in both tables - if a row in table A has no corresponding row in table B, it's excluded entirely. LEFT JOIN (or LEFT OUTER JOIN) returns all rows from the left table regardless of whether there's a match, and fills in NULLs for the right table's columns when there isn't one. A good mental image: INNER JOIN is the intersection of two circles in a Venn diagram, LEFT JOIN is the entire left circle plus the overlap. A practical example - if you join customers LEFT JOIN orders, you'll see every customer even if they've never placed an order, with NULL order fields. With INNER JOIN, customers with zero orders would just disappear from the results.
that's a good way to put it, thanks
Glad it clicked! The Venn diagram framing tends to stick better than memorizing the syntax rules.
explain tcp vs udp to me like I'm setting up a game server and need to actually decide

TCP guarantees delivery and ordering - packets are acknowledged, retransmitted if lost, and reassembled in the correct order before your application sees them, but that reliability comes with overhead and latency from handshakes and retransmission waits. UDP just fires packets without any guarantee they arrive, arrive in order, or arrive at all, but it has much lower overhead and latency since there's no acknowledgment or retransmission machinery. For a game server, the common pattern is to use UDP for real-time state like player position updates, since a slightly stale or dropped position packet just gets superseded by the next one a few milliseconds later and retransmitting an old position would be pointless. TCP or a reliable layer built on top of UDP is typically used for things that must arrive correctly, like chat messages, inventory changes, or match results, where losing or reordering a message would actually break something.
so is it common to use both at once in the same game?

Very common, yes - a lot of multiplayer games run a hybrid setup, using UDP as the primary channel for fast-moving gameplay state and either raw TCP or a custom reliability layer built over UDP for critical events. Some engines implement their own reliable-UDP protocol so they get the low latency of UDP but add selective acknowledgment and retransmission only for the packet types that actually need it, avoiding TCP's head-of-line blocking where one lost packet stalls delivery of everything queued behind it.

I'm rewriting my resume for a project coordinator role. Current bullet: "Responsible for scheduling meetings and taking notes for team." It feels weak. How do I make it sound more impactful without lying?

The core issue is that it describes a duty rather than an outcome, so it reads passive even though the actual work you did might have had real impact. Start by asking yourself what changed because you did this well: did meetings run more efficiently, did fewer things fall through the cracks, did stakeholders get clearer follow-ups? Even administrative-sounding work usually has a downstream effect worth naming. A rewrite might look like: "Coordinated scheduling and documentation for a cross-functional team of 8, ensuring action items from each meeting were tracked and completed on time." That keeps it truthful but reframes it around the point of the task, not just the mechanics. If you have any numbers, even rough ones, like number of recurring meetings managed per week, number of stakeholders, or percentage of action items closed on schedule, add them, since quantified bullets read as more credible and specific even to a skimming recruiter. Also swap passive constructions like "responsible for" for a strong action verb: coordinated, streamlined, maintained, tracked, synthesized. Small wording changes like this consistently make administrative work sound like project ownership rather than task execution, which is usually a more accurate reflection of what coordinators actually do day to day anyway.
Good point about the numbers. I don't have exact stats, is it okay to estimate?

Yes, reasonable estimates are standard practice and expected on resumes, as long as you're not fabricating something wildly implausible and could explain your reasoning if asked in an interview. If you managed meetings for a team you know had roughly 8 people meeting weekly for about 6 months, saying "coordinated logistics for 25+ weekly meetings across an 8-person cross-functional team" is a fair, defensible estimate, not a lie, since you can reconstruct that math from known facts. The line gets crossed when you invent outcomes you have no basis for, like claiming a specific percentage improvement in something you never actually measured. A safer wording for outcomes you believe happened but can't quantify is qualitative but specific language, like "reduced missed follow-ups by consistently tracking and circulating action items after each meeting," which conveys impact without a fake number attached to it. If you're ever unsure whether an estimate is reasonable, a good gut check is: could you explain out loud in an interview roughly how you arrived at that figure? If yes, it's fine to include. If you'd be caught flat-footed justifying it, round it down or switch to qualitative phrasing instead.
my docker builds are taking forever even for tiny code changes. how do I make better use of layer caching?

The most common fix is ordering your Dockerfile so things that change rarely come before things that change often. A typical mistake is copying your whole source tree before installing dependencies - that invalidates the dependency-install layer on every code change. Instead, copy just your package manifest first, run the install step, and only then copy the rest of the source. That way Docker can reuse the cached dependency layer as long as the manifest hasn't changed. Also worth checking: are you using multi-stage builds? And is your dockerignore file excluding things like .git, node_modules, or build artifacts that shouldn't be sent to the build context at all, since a large context alone can slow things down even before caching comes into play.
I do copy the whole tree first actually, let me reorder that. does the order of RUN commands matter for caching beyond that?

Yes - each RUN, COPY, and ADD instruction creates its own layer, and Docker caches based on the instruction plus its inputs up to that point. If any earlier layer changes, every layer after it gets invalidated too, even if that specific instruction's own inputs didn't change. So group commands that logically change together, and try to put the most stable, least-frequently-changing instructions as early as possible. Combining several RUN commands with && can also help reduce layer count if you don't need to cache them separately, though it's a tradeoff against build clarity.

I'm finally planning the northern lights trip I've wanted to do for years, probably Iceland or northern Norway. Before I book anything I want to actually understand what's happening in the sky, not just show up and go 'ooh pretty colors.' What's the real story behind why the aurora happens at all?

Good instinct, it makes the whole experience land differently when you know what you're actually watching. The sun constantly streams out charged particles in what's called the solar wind, and most of the time our planet's surrounding magnetic environment deflects the bulk of that stream harmlessly around us, which is honestly one of the quiet reasons life on the surface is viable at all. Near the poles, though, the geometry of that surrounding field funnels some of those particles down into the upper atmosphere instead of deflecting them away. When those particles slam into oxygen and nitrogen molecules high up, they transfer energy into them, and the molecules briefly glow as they shed that extra energy back off, similar in spirit to how a gas in a neon sign glows when it's excited by a current, just on a vastly bigger and less controlled scale.
That's why I've read the colors differ, right, like green versus that occasional red or purple people see in photos?

Exactly right. The color depends mostly on which gas is doing the glowing and at what altitude, since different molecules and different atmospheric densities release energy at different characteristic wavelengths. Oxygen at the more common lower altitudes tends to produce the classic green that dominates most aurora photos, while oxygen higher up, where the atmosphere is thinner, tends to produce a deeper red that shows up in stronger displays. Nitrogen contributes some of the blue and purple fringes people notice, especially near the lower edges of a curtain during particularly active nights. So a photo with multiple colors layered together is usually capturing several different altitudes and gases lighting up simultaneously during a strong event, not just one uniform glow.
That's exactly the kind of context I wanted before booking, thanks. Iceland is looking like the winner now mostly for flight convenience.

Solid reasoning, and either destination should deliver the real thing on a clear, active night. Once you land on Iceland, it's worth building in a couple of extra buffer nights rather than one single shot, since cloud cover and the sun's activity level both matter a lot and neither is fully predictable weeks out from booking.

My homemade sandwich bread keeps coming out really dense, especially in the middle third of the loaf. The crust and edges seem fine. Recipe is a basic yeast bread, nothing fancy. What's likely going wrong?

Density specifically concentrated in the middle/center of a loaf, while the outer parts are fine, is a fairly specific symptom that usually points to one of two causes rather than a general kneading or yeast problem, since a broad proofing or yeast issue would typically affect the whole loaf more evenly rather than just the center. First and most common: the center of the loaf just doesn't get as hot as quickly as the outer crust during baking, so if your loaf is on the larger side or your oven runs a bit cool, the center may not fully set and expand before the crust has already firmed up around it, trapping a denser, less risen middle inside an already-set exterior shell. Try dropping your oven temperature by about 25 degrees, and extending bake time slightly, giving the center more time to catch up before the crust fully hardens and locks in the loaf's structure. Second, and honestly the more common culprit for exactly this pattern: underproofing combined with oven spring concentrated unevenly, if your dough hasn't fully doubled before baking, the initial blast of oven heat causes rapid expansion (oven spring) mostly at the edges and top where heat penetrates first, while the denser, less-risen center doesn't get the same lift, baking into place before it ever properly expanded. Make sure your dough is genuinely doubled, using the poke test (press a finger in, if it springs back slowly and leaves a slight indent, it's ready, if it springs back instantly, it needs more time) rather than a fixed time estimate, since proofing time varies a lot with kitchen temperature.
I think I've definitely been underproofing based on a fixed time, not really checking. How long should I actually expect it to take, roughly?

It genuinely varies a lot with kitchen temperature, so a fixed universal number will mislead you, which is exactly the problem you just identified, but here's a useful range to calibrate against your own kitchen. At a warm room temperature, around 75-78F, a standard yeasted dough typically doubles in about 1 to 1.5 hours for the first rise. At a cooler room temperature, say 65-68F, common in many homes especially as seasons shift and heating patterns change, that same dough can easily take 2 to 3 hours to fully double, nearly double the time, purely from the temperature difference, which is likely a big part of why a fixed-time approach has been underproofing your bread if your kitchen runs on the cooler side. The second rise, after shaping, in the loaf pan, is usually shorter than the first, commonly 45 minutes to 1.5 hours depending on temperature, and you're looking for the dough to crest just slightly above the rim of the pan, alongside the same poke test for readiness. Rather than trusting a clock at all going forward, I'd suggest checking visually and with the poke test starting at around the 45 minute to 1 hour mark for whichever rise you're on, and just continuing to check every 15-20 minutes past that until it passes, rather than assuming a specific time will always be correct. If your kitchen is consistently on the cooler side, a really reliable trick is proofing dough inside your oven with just the oven light on (not the heat), which creates a warm, draft-free environment and makes rise times far more consistent and predictable trip to trip.

Getting into an argument in my band's group chat about single-coil versus humbucker pickups. One guy swears humbuckers just sound 'thicker' for no real reason, like it's just marketing. I feel like there's an actual physical reason but I can't articulate it. Can you settle this for the group chat?

There's a real physical story here, not just marketing. A pickup works by having your steel guitar strings vibrate near a magnet wrapped in fine wire coil, and that vibration disturbs the surrounding field enough to induce a small signal in the coil, which then gets amplified. A single-coil pickup is exactly that, one coil, and it tends to pick up a bright, articulate tone, but it's also prone to a persistent background hum from nearby electrical sources like lighting or transformers in the building, since the coil isn't just responding to your strings. A humbucker uses two coils wired in a way that their unwanted hum cancels out while the guitar signal from the strings reinforces, hence the name. That extra coil and different winding also changes the tonal character, generally producing a rounder, warmer, higher-output sound many players describe as thicker.
Okay so the hum-cancelling part I get, but does that actually explain the tone difference, or is the tone thing more just 'two coils equals more output equals sounds different'?

Good follow-up, and it's genuinely both factors layered together. Part of it is straightforwardly output level, two coils in that configuration generally produce a hotter signal than one, which can push an amp into breakup sooner and read as fuller or more saturated. But there's also a real tonal shaping effect independent of loudness: the two-coil arrangement and typical winding choices tend to roll off some of the highest frequencies compared to a single coil, which is part of why humbuckers get described as warmer or darker rather than just louder. So your bandmate isn't entirely wrong that a chunk of the perceived difference is about level and amp response, but there's also a genuine frequency-response difference baked into the coil geometry itself, so it's not pure marketing.
Perfect, that's a way better answer than anything I would've come up with. Sending screenshots to the chat now.

Good luck with that, pickup debates in guitar circles tend to be endless, but at least this version has some actual physics backing it instead of just vibes. If it comes up again, the coil-hum-cancellation history is a fun side note too, it was originally developed mainly to fix noise problems in recording studios, and the tonal character people love now was almost a side effect of that engineering fix rather than the original goal.

I was reading a biography of Michael Faraday last night and it kind of blew my mind that the guy had almost no formal math education but ended up laying the groundwork for basically all of electrical engineering. How does that even happen?

It really is one of the wilder stories in science history. Faraday came from a poor family, was apprenticed to a bookbinder as a teenager, and basically educated himself by reading the books he was binding. He got his big break by attending Humphry Davy's lectures at the Royal Institution and sending Davy his meticulous notes, which landed him a lab assistant job. What's fascinating is that his lack of formal math training might have actually helped him in some ways — he thought almost entirely in terms of physical pictures and "lines of force" rather than equations, which is part of why his notebooks are so intuitive to read even today. It was Maxwell who came along later and translated Faraday's physical intuition into the formal mathematical language of field equations. There's something almost poetic about it: one guy sees the physical reality with startling clarity, and another gives it the symbolic backbone. Davy reportedly said his greatest discovery was Faraday himself, which given everything Faraday went on to do for the world, might be underselling it.

Actually he did reasonably well by the standards of the time, which is nice to hear for once. He became the director of the Royal Institution's laboratory, was offered a knighthood (which he turned down twice on religious grounds, believing it conflicted with his humility as a Sandemanian Christian), and was given a house at Hampton Court by Queen Victoria to live in for free during his later years. He wasn't wealthy, but he wasn't destitute either, and he was genuinely famous in his own lifetime for his public lectures, especially the Christmas Lectures for young people that still run today. Where it gets a little bittersweet is that he refused to patent any of his discoveries, saying they belonged to everyone, so companies that built dynamos and motors off his principles made real fortunes while he lived comfortably but modestly. He apparently didn't seem to mind much, which either makes him a saint or means he just genuinely loved the tinkering more than the payoff.

I have a behavioral interview next week for a mid-level marketing role. I'm bad at the "tell me about a time you handled conflict" type questions, I always ramble. Any framework that helps?

The STAR framework is the standard fix for rambling and it works well precisely because it forces a fixed structure onto an open-ended memory, which is where rambling usually comes from, trying to recall and narrate simultaneously. Situation: one or two sentences of context, just enough for the interviewer to picture where you were, no more. Task: one sentence on specifically what you were responsible for or what problem needed solving, this is often skipped and its absence is a big source of rambling since listeners lose track of what the point of the story even is. Action: the longest section, but broken into specific steps you personally took, using "I" not "we" even in team situations, since interviewers are assessing your individual contribution. Result: end with a concrete outcome, ideally quantified, and if possible a brief reflection on what you learned or would do differently. For conflict questions specifically, pick a story where the conflict was resolved through your communication or problem solving, not one where you were simply right and someone else was wrong, since interviewers are listening for maturity and self awareness more than vindication. Practice this story out loud, timed, aiming for 90 seconds to 2 minutes total, since going over that is almost always where the rambling creeps back in.
I have a story in mind but it makes me look a little bad in the middle, I made an assumption that caused a delay. Is it risky to include that?

Including a real mistake is usually a strength, not a risk, as long as the story's arc moves toward resolution and growth rather than dwelling on the mistake itself, interviewers are generally more suspicious of candidates whose stories always paint them as flawless than of ones who show a genuine, recoverable misstep. The key is proportion: spend relatively little time on the mistake itself, just enough to set up the stakes, then spend more narrative weight on what you did once you realized the assumption was wrong, how you caught it, communicated it, and corrected course, and finish with the outcome and what changed in how you operate afterward, for instance now double-checking assumptions with stakeholders earlier in a project. This actually maps very well onto a conflict question if the delay caused friction with a colleague or client, since you can frame the "conflict" as the tension that arose from your assumption, and the resolution as how you addressed it directly rather than avoiding the person or getting defensive. One thing to avoid: don't over-apologize or self-deprecate in the telling, state the mistake plainly and matter of factly, then move quickly into the action and result, since dwelling too long on the error itself, even to be humble, can accidentally read as rambling again or lack of confidence, which is the exact problem you're trying to fix in the first place.

I watched a nature documentary last night about electric eels leaping partway out of the water to shock a horse model, apparently based on some old explorer's account. It seems almost too wild to be real. How do these animals actually generate a shock with just biological tissue?

That leaping behavior is real and was confirmed experimentally fairly recently, researchers built a fake alligator head wired to a meter and got eels to launch themselves at it in defensive tests, so the old explorer accounts weren't just tall tales. As for the mechanism, electric eels have specialized organs made of thousands of stacked cells called electrocytes, running most of the length of their body. Each individual electrocyte only produces a tiny voltage on its own, but because they're arranged in long series like cells in a battery pack, the small contributions add up. When the eel's nervous system triggers them to fire in synchrony, the combined effect is a jolt strong enough to stun prey or deter a predator, and the leaping behavior concentrates that jolt against a target instead of dissipating through open water.
So they're basically walking around with a built-in battery stack. Do they shock themselves too, or is there something that protects their own body from it?

That's one of the more interesting open questions in the biology. Eels do seem to have some degree of natural insulation and internal arrangement that reduces the effect on their own vital organs, and their electrocyte-heavy tail makes up a large fraction of their body length, keeping the bulk of the discharge running through that section rather than through more delicate organs near the head. That said, researchers have observed that eels aren't perfectly immune, repeated or prolonged discharges do seem to cause the animal some degree of exertion or stress, similar to how a person might tire out after a hard physical effort, just from a different underlying cause.
Wild. I had no idea this was an active area of actual research and not just settled textbook trivia.

It really is still active, partly because eels turn out to be a useful model organism for studying how biological tissue can be engineered into efficient, densely packed power-generating structures, which has inspired some soft-robotics and bio-inspired power source research. Worth looking up if the documentary sparked your interest, there's a decent trail of accessible science writing on it beyond the initial viral splash of the alligator-head study.

how are octopuses so smart despite being so different from vertebrates neurologically?

Octopus intelligence is a striking case of convergent evolution - complex cognition evolving independently along a completely separate evolutionary branch from vertebrates. Roughly two-thirds of an octopus's neurons aren't even in its central brain, they're distributed throughout its eight arms, giving each arm a significant degree of autonomous sensory processing and even localized decision-making, so an octopus can have an arm exploring a crevice and reacting to what it touches somewhat independently of the central brain's direct moment-to-moment control. This decentralized architecture is fundamentally different from the vertebrate model of a central brain issuing top-down commands through a spinal cord. Despite that structural difference, octopuses demonstrate behaviors associated with high intelligence in vertebrates - they can solve novel puzzles like unscrewing jar lids to get food, use tools such as carrying coconut shells for shelter, and show individual personality differences and apparent play behavior, all without anything resembling a vertebrate brain's architecture.
is there a leading theory for why that level of intelligence would evolve in a solitary short-lived animal?

This is actually one of the more debated puzzles in the field, since the usual evolutionary explanations for intelligence in vertebrates - long lifespans allowing learning to pay off, complex social structures requiring social cognition - largely don't apply to octopuses, which are mostly solitary and live only one to a few years. The leading hypothesis centers on their soft, shell-less bodies leaving them extremely vulnerable, which likely drove intense selective pressure for behavioral flexibility, camouflage strategies, and rapid problem-solving to evade predators and exploit varied food sources, essentially substituting cognitive flexibility for the physical armor or speed that many other prey animals rely on instead. It's considered a strong example of intelligence arising from ecological necessity and predation pressure rather than from the social or long-lifespan pathways that typically get discussed in vertebrate contexts.
